title: Practice English with this fun storytime read-along! Learn vocabulary & idioms! 📖
channel: Speak English with Bo's Slow English

lines.text: Hi everyone. Welcome to a new episode of
Bo's Slow English. This week we're doing
another read-along, but this time we
will be introducing some intermediate
vocabulary words. I will start by
reading the story at a normal pace, a
pace in which a native English speaker
would speak. And then we will break down
the story. I'll read it slower so you
can read it along with me, and I'll read
it one last time at a more moderate
pace. Before we get started, please give
me a like and subscribe to my channel.
It's your way of letting me know that
you are enjoying this content and I
appreciate all of your support. Ready to
start?
Jack lives in a busy city. He works in a
tall building downtown where he can see
the whole city from his office window.
Every morning he takes a quick walk to
get coffee. It's a daily habit that
helps him wake up. A cup of Joe, he
calls it, just like his dad used to.
One morning, while standing in line,
Jack sees an old friend, Sarah. They
haven't seen each other in ages, so he's
surprised to see her here.
"Long time no see," he says with a big
smile. They catch up on each others'
lives, talking about work, family, and
funny memories. They're both surprised
at how much time has passed. After they
finish their coffee, Jack invites Sarah
to join him for lunch. He says, "My
treat," which means he will pay for it.
They walk to a nearby restaurant and
find a quiet spot to sit. As they look
at the menu, Sarah mentions how fast the
city has changed. "Time flies," Jack
agrees. They both laugh, realizing that
they still remember this place from
years ago.
At lunch, Jack and Sarah talk about
their goals and dreams. Sarah shares her
plans to travel, while Jack mentions his
interest in learning a new language.
They encourage each other to follow
their dreams and not give up. "Better
late than never." Sarah says smiling.
They both leave lunch feeling inspired
and hopeful for the future. How was
that? A little bit fast? Well, I'm not
expecting for you to speak at that pace
just yet. Let's go over a few vocabulary
words. Downtown, the main business area
in a city. Habit, something you do often
like a routine. Catch up, to talk with
someone after a long time and share
what's new. My treat, a way of saying
you will pay for someone's food or
drink. Encourage, to give support and
confidence to someone. If you try to
create your own sentences using these
vocabulary words, it'll help you to
ingrain or stick in the brain.
There were a few idioms in the story
such as long time no see. This means
it's been a long time since you've seen
someone. Time flies. This means that
time passes very quickly. Better late
than never.
This means that it's better to do
something late than to never do it at
all. Did you notice a few homophones in
the story? Whole and hole. Whole means
complete or entire and hole is an empty
space.
There, there, and there. There shows
possession like their coffee. There is a
contraction of they are, and there
refers to a place or location. How about
the contractions in the story, such as
haven't, which is have not. They haven't
seen each other in ages. It's, it is.
It's a daily habit. Doesn't, does not.
It doesn't feel like that much time has
passed. Repeat these sentences after me
to practice. Jack and Sarah haven't seen
each other in a long time.
Time flies when you're with friends.
Better late than never, they say. Did
you notice that the word better, when
pronounced with an American English
accent, doesn't sound like two Ts put
together, it sounds like two Ds.
Better, not better.
And one last sentence to review
together. Jack's office has a whole view
of the city, and he loves it. Are you
ready to read the story with me at a
much slower pace? Let's do it.
